summaries.example: Imagine a town with one mayor who makes all the town’s rules. If there were two mayors with completely independent power, people might wonder whose rules to follow. Some philosophers use a similar idea when asking whether there can be more than one all-powerful God. They also ask whether the world’s order suggests one creator, while noting that order might also come from several cooperating powers.
summaries.summary: Monotheism is the view that there is one God. The entry first describes how some religious ideas may develop toward monotheism: a god is seen as creator of the world, greatest in power, and worthy of exclusive worship. It then examines several philosophical arguments for God’s uniqueness. One says that a simple God, whose important properties are not separate parts, could not have a second God beside him. Another says that a perfect God could not be distinguished from another equally perfect God. The entry finds difficulties in both arguments because God may have properties that depend on particular created things and are not essential. Stronger arguments begin with divine sovereignty, omnipotence, and total devotion. A unified world may suggest a unified cause, although it does not prove that there is only one creator. The entry also discusses how Kabbalah, Christianity’s Trinity, and Shri Vaishnavism address teachings that can seem to challenge divine unity.
key_ideas: Monotheism says that there is one God, understood as the ultimate creator and ruler.
Some arguments say that God’s simplicity or perfection would make two Gods impossible.
Other arguments begin with God’s rule over creation, unlimited power, or the demand for complete devotion.
The entry also explains that some religious traditions have teachings that seem to raise questions about how divine unity works.
These arguments are philosophical proposals, not claims that every thinker accepts.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question of monotheism is important because it asks what people mean when they call something “God.” It also shows how philosophers test a big idea from different directions: by thinking about perfection, power, causes, and worship. Studying the arguments helps readers understand both why monotheism has seemed reasonable to many thinkers and why some parts of the reasoning remain debated. It also encourages respectful learning about different religious traditions.

important_terms.definition: The belief that there is only one God.
A being’s power to make anything that is logically possible happen.
The idea that God is the complete cause of everything else that exists.
Giving someone complete love, loyalty, and commitment.
A feature that makes something good or excellent, such as wisdom or goodness.

questions_to_think_about: Would one orderly world be evidence for one creator, or could several creators work together?
Could two beings both be completely perfect, or would one have to be less perfect?
Can a person give complete devotion to two different beings?
How might a tradition explain several divine names, forms, or persons while still teaching that ultimate reality is one?

summaries.example: Suppose two beings are each claimed to be the total cause of every contingent thing—that is, every thing that could have failed to exist. If each is a sufficient cause in the strong sense, meaning that the being alone guarantees the existence of those things, then the other being is not needed as a necessary cause. The argument therefore seems to create a contradiction. But the reasoning depends on using “sufficient cause” consistently. A cause may be sufficient in an ordinary, conditional sense while still requiring other contributing conditions. This distinction is central to evaluating the sovereignty argument.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines monotheism as the claim that there is one God and asks whether God’s uniqueness can be established philosophically. Its historical discussion notes that Israelite religion may have developed from exclusive worship of Yahweh toward explicit monotheism, while similar tendencies can occur when worshippers elevate one deity to unlimited sovereignty. The first philosophical arguments appeal to divine simplicity and perfection. If all divine properties were identical or if God possessed every pure perfection and no other relevant properties, two Gods would seem impossible. The entry argues, however, that these premises are controversial. God appears to have real contingent properties, such as creating a particular person, and such properties may provide a possible way to distinguish beings. The argument from causal order observes that the world’s unified structure suggests a unified cause, though it does not by itself exclude cooperating designers. A more ambitious sovereignty argument says that God is the total cause of contingent reality, but it must distinguish weak from strong causal sufficiency. The omnipotence argument is stronger if distinct persons can necessarily have opposing wills: conflict would make each unable to accomplish what the other prevents. Finally, the argument from total devotion holds that the worship appropriate to God is unconditional and indivisible. The entry then asks how Kabbalistic emanations, the Christian Trinity, and Shri Vaishnava accounts of Vishnu and Lakshmi can be understood in relation to monotheism.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes historical movement toward exclusive worship from a strict philosophical proof that only one God can exist.
Arguments from simplicity and perfection depend on controversial assumptions about God’s properties and about how two beings could be distinguished.
The argument from causal order supports, at most, one controlling or cooperating source unless further reasoning rules out several causes.
The total-causality argument depends on whether divine activity is a necessary and sufficient cause in a weak or strong sense.
The omnipotence argument claims that two genuinely distinct, essentially omnipotent persons could have opposing wills, but neither could be thwarted.
The total-devotion argument says that worship, understood as unconditional commitment and life-centering devotion, cannot be completely divided between two distinct beings.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it connects a religious commitment with questions in metaphysics and logic: What makes a being divine? Can two beings share every essential perfection? What does it mean to be the complete cause of the world? The entry also demonstrates that “one God” can be interpreted in more than one way. A tradition may treat several names, attributes, manifestations, or persons as one reality rather than as separate gods. Examining these distinctions allows readers to compare arguments without assuming that one tradition’s interpretation settles the issue for all others.

important_terms.definition: The thesis that exactly one God exists, where God is understood as the ultimate divine reality.
The doctrine that God’s real properties are not separate parts and are identified with one divine being or nature.
A property that is good-making without implying limitation or defect, such as knowledge or power.
The status of having authority or causal rule over everything else that exists.
A condition that guarantees an outcome by itself, rather than merely helping produce it under additional conditions.
A property held in every possible situation in which a being exists.
A property a being has in some situations but could lack in others.
The logical or metaphysical possibility that there could be more than one divine person or being.

questions_to_think_about: Does a perfectly unified cosmos support one cause, or only coordinated causes?
Can the difference between essential and contingent properties rescue the simplicity or perfection arguments?
Is the concept of distinct persons compatible with wills that cannot conflict?
Does “ought implies can” strengthen the argument from total devotion, or are religious obligations more complicated?
How do the entry’s discussions of the Trinity and Lakshmi test different definitions of divine unity?

summaries.example: Imagine a computer game with one set of rules used everywhere. You might guess that one designer created the whole system. But several designers could have agreed on the same rules, so the game’s unity would not prove there was only one designer. Philosophers make a similar point about the universe. Its order may suggest one source or one guiding will, but extra reasoning is needed to show that several cooperating causes are impossible.
summaries.summary: Monotheism is the belief that there is one God. The SEP entry begins by looking at how this belief may arise. In ancient Israel, scholars describe an early stage in which other gods were not necessarily denied, but Israel was required to worship only Yahweh. Ideas about Yahweh as creator, greatest in power, and deserving exclusive worship could encourage a later belief that Yahweh alone is God. Similar patterns can occur when worshippers treat one deity as unlimited or supreme. The entry then studies arguments for God’s uniqueness. The simplicity argument claims that two simple Gods could not differ, since their important properties would be identical or equivalent. But simplicity is controversial, and contingent properties may leave room for differences. The perfection argument also faces trouble because not every property of God seems to be either a defect, a limited good, or a limitless perfection. Arguments from sovereignty are more promising. The universe’s order may suggest a single cause, though several cooperating causes remain possible. A stronger argument says that one God is the necessary and sufficient cause of everything else, but this depends on a careful meaning of “sufficient.” The omnipotence argument focuses on conflicting wills, while the total-devotion argument says that worship cannot be fully divided between two distinct beings. The entry closes by considering Kabbalah, Christianity, and Shri Vaishnavism, which each contain teachings that raise questions about how divine unity should be understood.
key_ideas: Some early religious developments connected creation, greatness, and exclusive worship with belief in one God.
The simplicity argument says two simple Gods could not differ, but it may overlook differences in contingent properties.
The perfection argument says two completely perfect beings would have no way to differ, but it relies on a disputed classification of properties.
The world’s unified order may point toward one designer or a unified plan, but it does not strictly rule out cooperation.
The omnipotence argument says two distinct all-powerful persons could not have conflicting wills without each limiting the other.
The devotion argument says that if God deserves unconditional commitment, complete devotion cannot be given to two separate beings.
summaries.why_it_matters: Monotheism matters because it is not only a religious label; it is also a question about the basic structure of reality. The arguments ask whether one ultimate source better explains the world than several sources and whether divine qualities such as perfection and unlimited power can belong to more than one being. The final sections show why definitions matter: ideas such as “person,” “attribute,” “manifestation,” and “one reality” can be understood differently in different traditions. Learning these distinctions supports careful and respectful comparison.

important_terms.definition: The view that there is one God rather than several gods.
The idea that God has no separate parts and that divine properties belong together in one divine reality.
A quality that makes a being better, such as wisdom, goodness, or power, without itself being a defect.
Complete rule or control over everything else that exists.
Having unlimited power, within what is logically possible.
A cause that is needed for an effect and, in the relevant sense, enough to bring it about.
A feature that a being must have in every possible situation where it exists.
Loyalty and commitment that place one being at the center of one’s life and cannot be divided without changing their meaning.

questions_to_think_about: Why might belief in a creator lead some people toward belief in one God?
What is the difference between a property a being must have and one it happens to have?
Could several powerful beings cooperate perfectly? What would that show?
Why might total devotion be different from ordinary admiration or loyalty?
How can a religious tradition explain several divine aspects while maintaining that ultimate reality is one?
